title: Argosy Health - Escalation / Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up to the 2026-11-18 production outage affecting Argosy Health's clinical summarization pipeline. Reviewed root cause (autoscaler/thundering herd + KV-cache eviction + retry amplification), mitigations deployed, and planned reliability improvements. Agreed next steps include a deep-dive benchmark, expanded observability, and a limited dedicated pilot for high-volume routes.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-25
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Avery, Samir, Lena (Redwood); Jordan, Priya, Markus, Tara (Argosy)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick recap, um we pushed the initial postmortem last week and wanted to walk through the RCA and the mitigations we actually put in place.
[00:18] Jordan: Yep, thanks. we had a pretty bad spike during monday's ingest window, about 3x normal qps, and the summarization jobs started failing with 5xx, latency ballooned.
[00:34] Priya: yeah and to add -- our side retried aggressively which amplified the load, there was a retry storm.
[00:48] Samir: So quick tl;dr from our infra analysis: there was a confluence of three things — the autoscaler decision window was aggressively tearing down idle workers, the KV-cache eviction threshold wasn't tuned for Argosy's long conversation prefixes so a lot of requests missed the cache, and the client-side retries caused concurrent retries all hitting the hosted pool, causing queuing and CPU saturation.
[01:06] Markus: (interrupting) so was this a bug in your autoscaler or an expected behavior we misconfigured?
[01:12] Samir: It's a combination. the autoscaler behavior is by design to free capacity, but our default policy didn't match Argosy's high-burst traffic pattern. we shipped a temporary change to the scaling hysteresis and reduced aggressive scale-to-zero behavior.
[01:28] Jordan: ok, that helped but the incident showed there's a bigger need for preferrable dedicated capacity for those routes.
[01:36] Avery: Right, which is why we proposed the small dedicated pilot for the clinical-summaries route; that would give you pinned capacity and reduce contention.
[01:45] Tara: can you remind us on the security surface — if we go dedicated, do we still get the same audit logs and KMS integration?
[01:52] Lena: Yes — Dedicated includes VPC peering options, KMS/HSM support, and the same audit logging; we can also enable longer retention for the console and ship logs to your Splunk instance.
[02:06] Priya: One question on KV cache: is the cache per-tenant or global? we saw a lot of cross-tenant eviction which hurt our tails.
[02:14] Samir: Today it's per-pool by default; we recommend a per-tenant pool for isolating hot prefixes. for the pilot we can configure a per-tenant cache with larger memory allocation so your long prefixes stay in cache.
[02:30] Jordan: About retries — is there a recommended client-side backoff we should adopt? our SDK currently retries 5 times aggressively.
[02:38] Avery: We suggest exponential backoff with jitter and reducing max retries to 2 for idempotent requests; also enabling circuit-breaker logic on your side reduces retry amplification. we can share a patched SDK snippet.
[02:52] Tara: Great. can you also provide the incident timeline in the format our audit team wants? they need a timeline, affected endpoints, user impact numbers, and mitigation steps.
[03:02] Avery: Yes, we'll send the formatted timeline and the consolidated logs.
[03:08] [03:15] Samir: On the immediate mitigations we applied during the incident: 1) increased the per-pool worker cap temporarily, 2) raised KV-cache memory thresholds, 3) throttled background non-critical jobs, and 4) adjusted autoscaler hysteresis to avoid scale-to-zero during peak windows. These reduced error rates from ~18% down to <1% during our tests.
[03:34] Jordan: Nice, are the mitigations permanent?
[03:38] Samir: We put some as temporary guardrails; we have a plan to bake them into a more robust autoscaler policy and expose config knobs to you for production.
[03:46] Priya: On the security front Markus raised a question about retained request bodies in logs for 90 days; that might be sensitive PHI.
[03:54] Lena: We can redact request bodies in the audit logs; we support field-level redaction and can integrate with your DLP workflow.
[04:02] Markus: we'll need formal confirmation of that and an SOC2/AICPA note.
[04:08] Avery: We'll send the compliance pack and answers to the specific audit questions.
[04:15] [04:30] Tara: On cost — if we go dedicated what's the rough per-month cost for the pilot?
[04:36] Lena: We'll post a pricing worksheet but ballpark for the small cluster we're recommending it's about $12k-$18k/month depending on SLA and burst options. We'll send the detailed worksheet.
[04:48] Jordan: Also can we run a controlled benchmark that mirrors our peak window?
[04:52] Samir: Yes, Samir: I'll run a dedicated benchmark with your dataset sample — p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, and token cost; we'll also simulate retry behaviors.
[05:02] Priya: Will the benchmark include KV-cache warmup? we've seen cold-cache performance is much worse.
[05:08] Samir: We'll run both cold and warm cache profiles and include a cache-warmup plan.
[05:14] [05:30] Conversation drifts to operational details with a few transcription artefacts here — filler words, overlapping talk: "uh", "yeah", etc.
[05:48] Avery: Quick recap: we'll send the postmortem, log links, and compliance pack; Samir will run the benchmark; Lena will send pricing; Jordan + Priya will provide dataset sample and list of peak windows; next call we'll review benchmark and pilot terms.
[06:03] Jordan: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[06:10] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcript had a few mis-attributions (Speaker 1/2 swaps) and some ASR confusions on technical acronyms (KV-cache sometimes transcribed as "K V cash").
